title: Miriam's timbrel (Exodus 15:20–21)
hook: the prophetess takes a drum and leads the women in dance

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of the Sea, and God hushing the angels. Your line was don't sing over the drowning. It's the end of a week: the plagues, a hard heart, the night of the firstborn, bread with no time to rise, the sea, the song. Day ninety-one.

Think about the last time you had to leave a place in a hurry. A fire alarm, a flight you nearly missed, a move that happened too fast. You grab what matters: keys, phone, the kids, maybe a photo. Now picture the night the Israelites left Egypt. They left so fast the bread didn't have time to rise. And yet, on the far shore of the sea, when the water has closed and the people are safe, one woman reaches into her bag and pulls out a drum. And then another woman does. And another. Somebody packed the drums. Today: Miriam, and the drum she brought.
screen: `LEAVING IN A HURRY.` → `NO TIME FOR THE BREAD TO RISE.` → `SOMEBODY PACKED THE DRUMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances." Three things in that one line. First, the title. Miriam is called a prophetess, the first woman in the Torah given that name. The rabbis ask why she's called the sister of Aaron and not of Moses, and the Talmud answers with a story: she was prophesying when she was only Aaron's sister, before Moses was even born, that her mother would have a son who would save the people. She's the girl who watched the basket on the Nile. Now she's leading a nation. Second, the drum. A timbrel is a hand drum, a frame with skin stretched over it, the kind you hold up and strike with your palm. And here's the question the midrash asks: where did these women get drums, in the desert, after leaving in such a rush? The answer, repeated by the great commentator Rashi, is that the women were so sure God would do wonders for them that they packed their drums in Egypt. They carried the celebration before there was anything to celebrate. Third, the song. Miriam sings a single line back to the women, "Sing ye to the LORD, for He is highly exalted", the same line Moses opened with. Moses sings the long song. Miriam gets everyone dancing. Both belong to the story. Many Jewish women today point to this verse when they sing, drum and lead in their own communities. And the lesson inside it is quiet and practical. Hope isn't only a feeling. Sometimes it's a thing you put in your bag.
screen: `MIRIAM, THE FIRST PROPHETESS.` · `A HAND DRUM, PACKED IN EGYPT.` · `ONE LINE, AND EVERYONE DANCES.` · `HOPE YOU PUT IN YOUR BAG.` · then, large: `AND ALL THE WOMEN WENT OUT AFTER HER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: move for one minute. If you can stand, stand. If you can't, your hands and shoulders will do. Tap a rhythm on your leg or the table, like a hand drum. Sway. Nod. Nobody is watching, and nobody is grading. Let the body say something the mouth doesn't need to. Then, for the second minute, be still, and notice your heartbeat, the drum you always carry. The bell holds the time.
Miriam's timbrel. A hand drum, carried out of Egypt by women who were sure they'd need it, and played on the far shore of the sea.
Your line: bring the drum. Today, bring one thing that makes joy easier to wherever you're going: a song, a snack to share, a good word. Pack it before you need it. Day ninety-one.

howItsDone: Miriam's song is read in synagogue with the Song of the Sea each year, and in many communities women mark it by singing and drumming together, some on the seventh day of Passover.

fork.setup: you're one of the women, packing to leave Egypt tonight. there's no time and almost no room. what goes in the bag?
options: nothing: you'll leave it all behind.
fork.reveal: the midrash says the women packed their drums, so sure of wonders that they carried the celebration before it came.

original.note: Hebrew: a hand drum, the timbrel Miriam played. the same word appears in the Psalms' lists of instruments.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman with a tambourine.
what it means: the first prophetess leads a whole people in dance on the far side of the sea.
what a scholar hears: the Mekhilta, and Rashi after it, asks where the drums came from and answers that the women brought them out of Egypt in trust.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 15:20 and 15:21 (punctuation of 15:21 may differ).

Drums packed in Egypt: Mekhilta (Shirata 10) and Rashi on 15:20. Confirm citation.
